title: What to Take Before Drinking: The Evidence-Based Pre-Drinking Stack
excerpt: What to take before drinking to feel better the next day: food, water, DHM dose and timing, electrolytes, B vitamins, ZBiotics, and the popular options that don't work.
metaDescription: What to take before drinking: DHM timing and dose, electrolytes, B vitamins, ZBiotics, food, and what doesn't work, like activated charcoal.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** nothing you swallow before a night out can cancel the effects of drinking too much. The things that make the biggest difference are boring: eat a real meal, drink water alongside alcohol, pace yourself, and drink less. On top of that foundation, a small "pre-drinking stack" can help at the margins: a DHM supplement taken shortly before or during your first drink, an electrolyte drink, and possibly a B-complex. Some popular options, like activated charcoal and "liver flush" products, don't do what they claim. This guide walks through each option, what the evidence actually shows, how to time it, and what to skip.

**The quick plan:** About an hour before you go out, eat a meal with protein, fat, and fiber. Around your first drink, take your DHM dose if you use it. Alternate every alcoholic drink with a glass of water. Before bed, drink a glass of water or an electrolyte drink, and if you use DHM, many people take a second dose then. Do **not** take Tylenol (acetaminophen) before or while drinking, and don't count on charcoal or detox products to protect you.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes general research and is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before using any supplement** if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver or kidney disease, take prescription medicines (especially sedatives, blood thinners, antidepressants, seizure medicines, or diabetes drugs), or have been told not to drink. No supplement makes it safe to drive after drinking or to drink more than you otherwise would. If someone is confused, vomiting repeatedly, breathing slowly, or can't be woken, call 911 (US) right away.

## Why "What to Take Before Drinking" Is the Right Question (and Its Limits)

Most hangover advice focuses on the morning after, when the damage is done. Thinking ahead makes more sense, because almost everything that drives a hangover starts while you're drinking:

- **Alcohol and its by-products.** Your liver turns alcohol (ethanol) into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound, and then into harmless acetate. When acetaldehyde builds up faster than you clear it, you feel worse.
- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate more than you drink.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster but fragments the second half of the night, which leaves you groggy.
- **Inflammation and stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and triggers an immune response that researchers think contributes to the "sick" feeling of a hangover.
- **Congeners.** Darker drinks like bourbon, red wine, and brandy contain more of these fermentation by-products, which seem to make hangovers worse in some people.

Here is the limit you need to keep in mind. When researchers have reviewed the evidence for hangover remedies as a whole, the conclusions have been sobering. A systematic review in the *BMJ* (Pittler, Verster and Ernst, 2005) found no compelling evidence that any remedy prevented or treated hangovers. A larger review in *Addiction* (Roberts and colleagues, 2022) reached a similar verdict: some remedies showed hints of benefit, but the studies were small and the evidence was low quality. The single most reliable way to avoid a hangover is to drink less. Everything below is about helping at the margins, not giving you a free pass.

For the full prevention playbook, including pacing, sleep, and drink choice, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover). This page focuses on the specific question of what to take beforehand.

## The Pre-Drinking Stack at a Glance

| What to take | When | Evidence strength | Our take |
|---|---|---|---|
| A real meal (protein, fat, fiber) | 30 to 60 minutes before | Strong for slowing absorption | The most effective step on this list |
| Water | Before, and between every drink | Good common sense, modest research | Free and always worth it |
| DHM (dihydromyricetin) | Shortly before or with your first drink; optional second dose before bed | Promising animal research, limited human data | Our top supplement pick, with realistic expectations |
| Electrolyte drink | Before bed or the next morning | Helps with fluid loss, not the whole hangover | Useful, especially in heat or after dancing |
| B-complex vitamin | With your pre-drinking meal | Weak to modest | Low-cost, low-risk, small expected effect |
| ZBiotics (engineered probiotic) | Before your first drink | No published human hangover trial we can find | An option with real uncertainty |
| Prickly pear extract | Several hours before | One small human trial | Possible add-on |
| Activated charcoal | Not recommended | Doesn't bind alcohol well | Skip it |
| "Liver flush" or detox products | Not recommended | No good evidence | Skip it |
| Tylenol (acetaminophen) | Never before or while drinking | Clear safety concern | Avoid |

## Step 1: Eat a Real Meal Before You Drink

If you only do one thing on this page, do this. Food in your stomach slows the rate at which alcohol moves into your small intestine, which is where most of it gets absorbed. That means a lower and later peak in blood alcohol, and more time for your liver to keep up.

This is one of the better-studied ideas in this whole area. Forensic researchers, including A.W. Jones and colleagues in Sweden, have shown in controlled studies that drinking after a meal produces noticeably lower peak blood alcohol than drinking the same amount on an empty stomach. The effect isn't small, and it doesn't depend on any special food. A normal meal works.

**What to eat:**

- **Protein:** chicken, fish, eggs, beans, Greek yogurt. Protein takes longer to digest and helps keep your stomach full.
- **Healthy fats:** avocado, nuts, olive oil, salmon. Fat slows stomach emptying.
- **Fiber-rich carbs:** whole grains, potatoes, vegetables, fruit. These help keep blood sugar steadier, and low blood sugar can make you feel worse the next morning.
- **Salty foods in moderation:** a bit of salt helps you hold onto fluid.

**Timing:** eat within about an hour before your first drink. A snack at the bar helps a little, but it isn't a substitute for a meal.

For specific meal ideas, see our full guide on [what to eat before drinking alcohol](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide).

## Step 2: DHM, the Supplement Most Worth Considering

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound found in the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*), which has a long history of use for drinking in traditional Chinese and Korean medicine. It's the main ingredient in most of the hangover supplements we cover on this site.

### What the research shows

The case for DHM rests mostly on animal and lab research, with limited human data. That matters, so here is what we know:

- **Brain effects in rats.** A study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* (Shen and colleagues, 2012) found that DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal in rats. The researchers linked this to DHM's action on GABA-A receptors, the same brain receptors alcohol acts on.
- **Liver and alcohol metabolism in mice.** A study in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* (Silva and colleagues, 2020) reported that DHM improved markers of alcohol metabolism in mice, including enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde, and reduced fat buildup in the liver.
- **People with fatty liver.** A small randomized trial in adults with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, published in *Pharmacological Research*, found improvements in some liver and metabolic markers with DHM compared with placebo. That study was not about hangovers or drinking, but it does offer some human data on safety and liver effects.

What's missing is a large, well-designed human trial testing whether DHM reduces hangover symptoms. Many users report that it helps, and the mechanism is plausible, but you should treat it as a reasonable bet, not a sure thing.

### DHM dose and timing before drinking

- **Dose:** most products contain 300 mg to 1,000 mg of DHM per serving. There is no officially established human dose for hangovers. Many people start around 300 to 600 mg for a moderate night and use more for a longer night, staying within the product label.
- **When to take it:** shortly before or with your first drink is the most common approach. Some people split the dose and take a second serving before bed, with a glass of water.
- **With food:** taking it with your pre-drinking meal is fine and may be easier on your stomach.

Timing questions are covered in detail in our [DHM timing guide](/never-hungover/when-to-take-dhm-timing-guide-2025), and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) and [dosage calculator](/dhm-dosage-calculator) help you work out an amount based on your body weight and how much you plan to drink.

### Which DHM product?

If you want to try DHM, two options we've reviewed are [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines 1,000 mg of DHM with L-cysteine, milk thistle, B vitamins, and electrolytes in one serving, and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), which is a simpler DHM-focused option. Our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare more brands on dose, price, and purity.

### DHM safety notes

DHM is generally well tolerated in the studies that exist, but long-term human safety data are limited. A few cautions:

- It may interact with medicines that are processed by the liver or that act on GABA receptors, such as benzodiazepines and some sleep aids. See our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) and check with a pharmacist if you take prescription drugs.
- It has not been studied in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
- It does **not** lower your blood alcohol level in any way that makes driving safe, and it is not a reason to drink more.

## Step 3: Hydration and Electrolytes

Alcohol makes you lose more fluid than you take in, mainly by blocking vasopressin. Dehydration contributes to thirst, dry mouth, headache, and fatigue the next day.

That said, dehydration is only part of the picture. Researchers have found that hangover severity doesn't track closely with measures of dehydration, which suggests other factors (acetaldehyde, inflammation, sleep loss) do a lot of the work. So hydration helps, but it isn't a cure.

**How to hydrate before and during drinking:**

- **Before you go out:** drink a glass or two of water with your meal. Arriving already a bit dehydrated, say after a workout or a hot day, makes things worse.
- **During:** alternate every alcoholic drink with a glass of water. This also slows your drinking, which may be its biggest benefit.
- **Before bed:** have a glass of water or an electrolyte drink.

**Do you need electrolytes, or is water enough?** For a normal night, water plus food is usually enough. An electrolyte drink (an oral rehydration solution or a sports drink) makes more sense if you've been sweating, dancing, out in the heat, or if you've been vomiting. Oral rehydration solutions have more sodium and less sugar than most sports drinks, which is closer to what your body needs to absorb water. We compare the main options in [Pedialyte vs Gatorade for hangovers](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) and our roundup of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks).

Taking electrolytes *before* drinking isn't harmful, but most people get more from having them before bed or the next morning, when fluid loss has actually happened.

## Step 4: B Vitamins (and Other Vitamins Before Drinking)

People often ask what vitamins to take before drinking. B vitamins come up most, for a few reasons. Alcohol interferes with how your body absorbs and uses several B vitamins, including thiamine (B1), folate, and B6. Heavy, long-term drinkers can develop real deficiencies, and thiamine deficiency in particular can cause serious brain problems.

**What the evidence says for hangovers:**

- An older small trial from the 1970s tested pyritinol, a synthetic relative of vitamin B6, and reported fewer hangover symptoms. It has not been well replicated, and pyritinol isn't the same as the B6 in a regular supplement.
- A study in the *Journal of Clinical Medicine* (Verster and colleagues, 2019) looked at people's normal diets and found that those who ate more nicotinic acid (a form of vitamin B3) and zinc tended to report less severe hangovers. That was an observational study based on what people reported eating, so it can't prove the vitamins caused the difference.

**Our take:** a standard B-complex with your pre-drinking meal is inexpensive and low-risk. The expected benefit for any single night is small. The stronger reason to keep your B vitamins up is if you drink regularly, because that's where real deficiencies happen. Stick to label doses: very high doses of B6 taken over long periods can cause nerve problems, and high-dose niacin can cause flushing and, rarely, liver strain.

**Other vitamins people ask about:**

- **Vitamin C:** important for overall health, but there's no good evidence it prevents hangovers.
- **Zinc:** linked to milder hangovers in the observational study above. A normal diet or a standard multivitamin is a reasonable way to cover it.
- **Magnesium:** heavy drinking can lower magnesium, and some people find it helps with sleep. There's no direct hangover research worth citing.

Many combination hangover products, including some DHM formulas, already include a B-complex and electrolytes, so check the label before you stack separate pills on top.

## Step 5: The ZBiotics Option

**ZBiotics** is a probiotic drink made from a bacterium (*Bacillus subtilis*) that has been genetically engineered to produce an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde. The idea is that the bacteria break down some acetaldehyde in your gut before it causes trouble. The company recommends drinking it before your first alcoholic drink.

**What to know before you try it:**

- **The idea is interesting.** The engineering is real, and the target (acetaldehyde) is a sensible one.
- **The evidence is thin.** As of this writing, we haven't found a published, peer-reviewed human trial showing ZBiotics reduces hangover symptoms. The company points to its own research and customer feedback.
- **The gut question.** Most acetaldehyde is made in your liver, not your gut. A probiotic working in the gut may only affect a portion of the total.
- **Price.** It costs more per night than most DHM products.

User reviews are mixed. Some people say it clearly helps; others notice nothing. If you're curious, it's reasonable to try it on a night you'd drink anyway and judge for yourself. We dig into the details in our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) and compare the two approaches in [DHM vs ZBiotics](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-zbiotics).

## Other Supplements People Take Before Drinking

These come up often in "supplements to take before drinking" lists. Here's an honest rundown.

### Prickly pear extract

A small human study in the *Archives of Internal Medicine* (Wiese and colleagues, 2004) found that prickly pear (*Opuntia ficus-indica*) extract taken several hours before drinking reduced some hangover symptoms, particularly nausea and dry mouth, and lowered a marker of inflammation. It's one of the few remedies with any human trial behind it, though it was a single small study. See [DHM vs prickly pear](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-prickly-pear-hangovers) for how the two compare.

### NAC (N-acetylcysteine)

NAC is a building block for glutathione, the liver's main antioxidant, and is used in hospitals to treat acetaminophen overdose. Some people take it before drinking on the theory that it helps the body handle acetaldehyde. Human hangover data are limited and mixed. Our [NAC vs DHM comparison](/never-hungover/nac-vs-dhm-which-antioxidant-better-liver-protection-2025) explains the evidence. NAC can cause stomach upset, and anyone with asthma or taking nitroglycerin should check with a doctor first.

### Milk thistle

Milk thistle (silymarin) is the most-studied liver herb. Human evidence for liver benefits is mixed, and there's no good evidence it prevents hangovers. It's included in some combination products, which is fine, but it's not a reason to buy one on its own for a night out.

### Ginger

Ginger has decent evidence for nausea in other settings, such as pregnancy and motion sickness. If nausea is your main hangover symptom, ginger tea or capsules the next morning are a sensible, low-risk choice. There's little reason to take it before drinking.

### Red ginseng and other herbal blends

There's some small-scale research on Korean red ginseng and on various herbal blends, mostly from single studies. Treat these as experimental. Herbal blends with many ingredients also make it harder to know what you're actually taking and at what dose.

For a broader look at how these compare, see our [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025), and if you want to combine several, our [DHM supplement stack guide](/never-hungover/dhm-supplement-stack-guide-complete-combinations) covers sensible pairings.

## What Does NOT Work (or Isn't Worth It)

This is where a lot of money gets wasted. These products are heavily marketed for pre-drinking use, but the evidence doesn't back them up.

### Activated charcoal

Activated charcoal is used in hospitals to bind certain poisons in the stomach. It's often sold as a "pre-party" pill on the idea that it will soak up alcohol. The problem is that charcoal binds alcohol poorly, and alcohol is absorbed quickly, so very little would be caught even if it did. Poison control guidance doesn't recommend charcoal for alcohol poisoning for this reason.

Charcoal also has real downsides. It can bind to medicines you take at the same time, including birth control pills and other prescriptions, making them less effective. It can cause constipation and black stools. Our [activated charcoal hangover guide](/never-hungover/activated-charcoal-hangover) goes into the details.

### "Liver flushes" and detox cleanses

"Liver flush" and "detox" products promise to prepare your liver for a night out or clean it up afterward. Your liver doesn't need to be flushed. It clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, and no cleanse speeds that up in a meaningful way. Some flush protocols, especially ones involving large amounts of oil and Epsom salts, can cause diarrhea, cramping, and fluid loss, which is the opposite of what you want before drinking. Some detox teas also contain laxatives or diuretics that make dehydration worse. We break down the marketing claims in our [liver detox guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-detox-science-based-methods-vs-marketing-myths-2025).

### Tylenol (acetaminophen) before drinking

Taking Tylenol before or during drinking to "get ahead" of the headache is a bad idea. It doesn't prevent a hangover, and it adds work for your liver at a time when it's already busy with alcohol. The combination is a well-known route to liver injury, especially for people who drink heavily on a regular basis. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the liver chemistry and safe timing.

### Ibuprofen, aspirin, and naproxen before drinking

These are easier on the liver but harder on the stomach. Alcohol already irritates your stomach lining, and adding an anti-inflammatory painkiller before drinking increases the risk of irritation and bleeding. If you need one the next morning, take it with food and water. You can read more in our guide to [Aleve and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol).

### Antacids and "Asian flush" pills

Some people take acid-reducing medicines like Pepcid (famotidine) to reduce alcohol flushing, the red face some people get when they drink. This hides the flush but doesn't fix the cause, which is a buildup of acetaldehyde from a common genetic variant in the ALDH2 enzyme. Hiding that warning sign can make it easier to drink more while acetaldehyde stays high. If you flush, read our [Asian flush guide](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) before reaching for a pill.

### Pepto Bismol beforehand

Pepto Bismol can help with an upset stomach the next day, but taking it before drinking doesn't prevent a hangover. There are also some interactions to know about, which we cover in [Pepto Bismol and alcohol](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol).

### Hangover patches

Patches that claim to deliver vitamins through your skin during a night out have very little research behind them, and it's unclear how much of their contents actually gets absorbed. See [do hangover patches work](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work) for the full look.

## A Simple Pre-Drinking Timeline

Here's how the pieces fit together on a typical night out.

**60 to 90 minutes before:**
- Eat a full meal with protein, fat, and fiber.
- Drink one or two glasses of water.
- Take a B-complex with the meal if you use one.

**Around your first drink:**
- Take your DHM dose if you use it.
- If you use ZBiotics, drink it now.
- Order a glass of water alongside your first drink.

**During the night:**
- Alternate each alcoholic drink with water.
- Aim for no more than about one standard drink per hour. Your liver clears roughly one per hour, though this varies from person to person.
- Lighter drinks like vodka, gin, and white wine tend to cause milder hangovers than darker ones like bourbon and red wine. A study in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* (Rohsenow and colleagues, 2010) found bourbon produced worse hangovers than vodka at the same blood alcohol level. Our [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) page covers what actually matters about drink order.
- Snack if the night runs long.

**Before bed:**
- Drink a glass of water or an electrolyte drink.
- Take a second DHM serving if that's part of your routine.
- Skip the Tylenol.

**The next morning:**
- Rehydrate, eat something, and rest. If you need a painkiller, choose carefully and take it with food.

## Who Should Skip the Supplements and Talk to a Doctor First

Supplements aren't right for everyone. Check with a doctor or pharmacist before trying any pre-drinking supplement if you:

- Are pregnant, trying to become pregnant, or breastfeeding (and in these cases, the safest choice is not to drink).
- Have liver disease, kidney disease, or have been told your liver enzymes are high.
- Take prescription medicines, especially sedatives, sleep aids, antidepressants, seizure medicines, blood thinners, or diabetes drugs.
- Take any prescription drug that carries a "do not drink alcohol" warning. No supplement changes that warning.
- Find that you need a "stack" to get through most weekends. Needing a routine to cope with regular heavy drinking is a sign it's worth talking to a doctor about the drinking itself. In the US, the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) is free, confidential, and open around the clock.

## The Bottom Line

The best things to take before drinking are a meal and a glass of water. After that, DHM is the supplement we think is most worth trying, with the honest caveat that the strongest evidence comes from animal studies. Electrolytes help with fluid loss, B vitamins are a low-cost and low-risk add-on, and ZBiotics is an interesting option with thin published evidence. Activated charcoal, liver flushes, and Tylenol before drinking are worth skipping. And no combination of pills will do as much as drinking less and slower.

If you want to go deeper, start with our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) and the full [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What should I take before drinking to avoid a hangover?**

Start with a real meal and water, which do more than any pill. If you want a supplement, DHM taken shortly before or with your first drink is the most commonly used option, with promising animal research and limited human data. An electrolyte drink before bed and a B-complex with your meal are reasonable add-ons. Nothing guarantees you'll avoid a hangover; drinking less is the most reliable method.

**What supplements should I take before drinking?**

The most commonly used are DHM, a B-complex, and electrolytes. Prickly pear extract has one small human trial behind it, and NAC and milk thistle are sometimes added, though their hangover evidence is limited. ZBiotics is an engineered probiotic taken before drinking, but we haven't found a published human hangover trial for it. Check with a pharmacist if you take prescription medicines.

**When should I take DHM before drinking?**

Most people take DHM shortly before or with their first drink. Some split the dose and take a second serving before bed with a glass of water. Typical product servings range from 300 mg to 1,000 mg. There is no officially established human dose for hangovers, so follow the product label.

**Does activated charcoal prevent hangovers?**

No. Activated charcoal binds alcohol poorly, and alcohol is absorbed too quickly for charcoal to catch much of it. Charcoal can also bind to medicines like birth control pills and make them less effective. It's not recommended before drinking.

**What vitamins should I take before drinking?**

A standard B-complex is the most sensible choice, since alcohol interferes with B vitamin absorption. An observational study linked higher dietary intake of vitamin B3 and zinc with milder hangovers, but that doesn't prove the vitamins caused it. Expect a small effect at most, and stay within label doses.

**Can I take Tylenol before drinking to prevent a headache?**

No. Acetaminophen before or during drinking doesn't prevent a hangover and adds extra work for your liver while it's processing alcohol. If you have a headache the next morning, eat first, make sure the alcohol has cleared, and take a single standard dose, or ask a pharmacist which option suits you.

**Is it better to take electrolytes before or after drinking?**

Both are fine, but most people get more from electrolytes before bed or the next morning, after fluid loss has happened. Before drinking, water with a meal is usually enough. Electrolyte drinks are most useful if you've been sweating, dancing, in the heat, or vomiting.

**Does ZBiotics work?**

It might, but the evidence is thin. ZBiotics uses a bacterium engineered to break down acetaldehyde in the gut. The idea is sound, but most acetaldehyde is made in the liver, and we haven't found a published peer-reviewed human trial showing it reduces hangovers. User reviews are mixed.
